To understand the new three-tier iPhone ecosystem is to understand a structure of deliberate digital segregation. Apple has fractured its user base along lines of hardware age, spending power, and how quickly you adopt new tech. It's no longer about owning an iPhone; it's about which class of iPhone you can afford to stay in.
At the bottom of this new hierarchy are the grandfathered iPhones. Apple boasts that iOS 27 supports legacy devices all the way back to the iPhone 11. But if you own a standard iPhone 15 or older, you get opti-mizations, not new features. Look past the faster app launches, and you'll realize your phone isn't getting smarter. You are locked out of the Siri Al workspace.
The middle tier would be any more recent iPhone, such as the 15 Pro, the base iPhone 16 or 17, and so on. But the fragmentation doesn't stop at artificial intelli-gence. iOS 27 introduces a variant of the OS that's strictly designed to reward the highest spenders. At the apex of this hierar-chy, in the highest tier, is the newly unveiled iPhone Duo class.

For years, Apple power users have practically begged for basic productivity features, such as the ability to run two applications simultaneously. Apple repeatedly restricted the feature, treating split-screen multitasking as a sacred boundary reserved only for the iPad or a desktop.
But the adaptive version of iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo shatters that philosophy. Unfold the Duo's massive canvas, and iOS 27 unlocks native, side-by-side app multitasking with unique app-pairing engines. By gating a baseline software feature like split-screen multitasking behind an eye-watering price tag, Apple is sending a clear mes-sage: Basic digital efficiency is no longer an inherent part of the smartphone experience.
Instead, it's an upmarket luxury.
